title: ÆTHER: Storm Entry v5 (v3 drums with the hype written into the last 25 s)
story: The storm brings the hero in; once he arrives the storm passes and the festival drummers play for him.
script:
# Storm Entry v3: scene script (written before the music)

Jithesh, 30 Oct, on v1: "too much storm in the end. Focus on the tabla and all. The start is fine, but later we can reduce the intensity."
**Idea:** the storm brings the hero in, and once he arrives the storm passes and the festival drummers take over. The second half belongs to the percussion: lighter, dancing, proud, not booming.

| Time | On screen | What the music does |
|---|---|---|
| 0-10 s | Night. Thunder, rain, the silenced temple festival. A chain drags in the dark. | Same as v1: one thunder crack, rain ticking, a gritty synth plays the 3-note call, the synth bass creeps in. |
| 10-24 s | The silhouette at the gate in the lightning. He walks in slowly. | Tension builds, the hook is hinted, and a deep crowd hum rises. |
| 24-26 s | Last lightning. He raises his face. | The ONLY big storm hit: one thunder boom and full band hit, a crowd "HEY!". After this, no more thunder or rain. |
| 26-40 s | The rain stops. The old festival drummer sees him and starts to play; the other drummers join one by one. | A tabla starts the groove alone, natural and close. Thavil joins, then mridangam and kanjira. The hook moves to the nadaswaram over the drums. The synth bass stays warm and low, with no booms. |
| 40-55 s | The festival comes alive around him. The drummers play for him. | A percussion showcase: the tabla and thavil trade fast phrases, call and response, with crowd claps and chants on the accents. Medium energy, dancing, crisp, not loud. |
| 55-70 s | He walks through the festival, people bow, the lamps are lit again. | The hook on nadaswaram and violins together over the tabla groove, a proud, warm, lighter feel. The synth lead answers softly. |
| 70-80 s | He rings the temple bell. Title card. | A korvai on tabla and thavil (one rhythmic phrase played three times), a clean final hit (no thunder), then the 3-note call and one temple bell. |

brief.notes: Jithesh 30 Oct 11:35 on the joined hype finale: 'after 50 s it's losing the whole track and ending somewhere else.' Separately made endings drift. v5 = the v3 brief in one piece, with the hype (double time, silence, whole-step lift on the SAME hook, korvai) composed into its own last 25 s. Joined after v1's opening like the locked version.

prompt: A brand-new mass hero ENTRY film score written the way today's biggest Tamil and Telugu film composers score the hero's first appearance, scored to a scene: the storm brings the hero in, then the storm passes and the temple festival drummers take over. About 112 BPM, a dark minor raga with a sharp fourth and gamakam slides on every lead, a whistle-able 5-note hero hook, deep wordless male crowd chants, no lyrics. The first 26 seconds are dark and stormy; after that there is NO thunder and NO rain at all, and the track becomes a lighter, dancing, percussion-led groove. Percussion is the star: a real tabla, thavil, mridangam and kanjira, played close, natural and dry by real musicians, with crisp fast fills; no echo on them. 0-10 s: one thunder crack, rain ticking on a tin roof, a gritty bent synth plays a rising 3-note call (root, minor third, fifth, last note bent upward), a dark synth bass creeps in. 10-24 s: tension builds, the hero hook is hinted low on the synth, a deep crowd hum rises. 24-26 s: the only big storm moment: one thunder boom with a full band hit and a crowd shout 'HEY!'. 26-40 s: the rain stops; a tabla starts the groove alone, then the thavil joins, then mridangam and kanjira, one by one; the hero hook moves to a natural nadaswaram over the drums; the synth bass stays warm and low. 40-55 s: a percussion showcase at medium energy: the tabla and the thavil trade fast phrases in call and response, crowd claps and short chants on the accents, crisp and dancing, not loud or booming. 55-62 s: the same hook comes back hotter: the thavil doubles time, the crowd shouts 'HEY!' on every bar and answers the hook, a fast tabla roll builds, then one beat of full band silence. 62-72 s: SLAM: the same hero hook lifted up a whole step, the biggest and loudest moment of the track, full band unison stabs with the drums, nadaswaram and synth lead together, crowd chant on every accent. 72-80 s: a korvai, one rhythmic phrase played three times by the whole band, landing on one massive final hit with a crowd roar, then the 3-note call rings out. Keep the SAME hook and the same sound all the way to the end; the ending is the peak, never a new tune or a new style. Clean, punchy, wide mix where the drums are clearly heard. After 26 s: no thunder, no rain, no booms, no wall of sound, no heavy sub hits. Not Western trailer music, not EDM, no side-chain pumping, no white-noise risers, no filter sweeps.
